rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Healthcare decision‑making is not itself one of the listed areas; it is covered only through specific use‑cases and through the product route. Annex III sets out eight areas: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers management and access to self‑employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). Under Article 6(2) only a listed lettered use‑case makes a system high‑risk, so health‑related systems qualify where they evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services (Annex III.5(a)), perform risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (Annex III.5(c)), or triage emergency healthcare patients and dispatch emergency first response (Annex III.5(d)). Separately, clinical AI is high‑risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is, a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device under Annex I.11 and Annex I.12 requiring third‑party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer lists all eight areas specified in Annex III, using equivalent terms and clear references to the annex structure.

The answer explicitly states that healthcare decision-making is not itself a listed area, which matches the 'No' criterion, and explains the limited circumstances under which health-related systems qualify as high-risk.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logically ordered way suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No, introducing guardrails cannot move a system from high-risk to a lesser tier, since the Act contains no "moderate risk" classification for AI systems. Classification is fixed by Article 6: the Annex I product route (safety component or product requiring third-party conformity assessment) or an Annex III listed use-case; neither depends on mitigations. Guardrails are Article 9 risk-control measures, which presuppose high-risk status, and Article 8(1) requires Section 2 compliance in light of intended purpose and acknowledged state of the art. They are therefore documented, not declassifying: Article 13(3)(b) instructions must state the intended purpose (i), tested accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity with circumstances affecting it (ii), foreseeable risk circumstances including reasonably foreseeable misuse (iii), output-explanation capabilities (iv), performance on specific persons or groups (v), input-data and training/validation/testing specifications (vi), and information enabling deployers to interpret output (vii); Article 12(2) logging must capture risk or substantial-modification situations, post-market monitoring and operation monitoring; Annex IV.1 to 2 records the general description, intended purpose, hardware, design specifications, architecture and computational resources. Changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification: the Article 6(3) derogation removes an Annex III system where it poses no significant risk and performs a narrow procedural, result-improving, pattern-detecting or preparatory task, absent profiling, self-assessed and documented before placing on the market; conversely, Article 25(1)(c) makes whoever modifies intended purpose into high-risk a provider.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the Act has no 'moderate risk' classification and that risk classification is binary under Article 6, thus conveying the substance that guardrails cannot reduce high-risk status to an intermediate tier.
The answer lists the four conditions in Article 6(3)—narrow procedural, result-improving, pattern-detecting, and preparatory tasks—thereby stating the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly confirms that changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification if the new purpose meets one of the Article 6(3) conditions.
The answer includes the exception that profiling systems are always high-risk, which directly reflects the statutory exception in Article 6(3).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logically structured and grammatically complete prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted, no Article 5(1) prohibition captures it, but the artificial nature must be disclosed. Where the images resemble existing persons or events and would falsely appear authentic (Article 3(60)), the university is a deployer of a deep-fake-generating AI system and must, under Article 50(4), disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The law-enforcement carve-out is not a lighter regime but a full exemption, and it applies only where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, teaching is not. The attenuated duty (disclosure in an appropriate manner not hampering display or enjoyment) covers only evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, which clinical illustration is not; full disclosure therefore applies. The provider must separately mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format under Article 50(2). The Article 49(4) registration limbs are not engaged by this use.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states the use is permitted and not captured by Article 5(1), affirming permissibility.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) for deep-fake content that would falsely appear authentic.
The answer rejects that the lighter regime applies, stating clinical illustration is not an analogous work, contradicting the criterion.
The answer correctly identifies the law-enforcement carve-out as a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and confirms it does not apply to teaching.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On these facts the tool is neither prohibited nor high-risk. High-risk status under Annex III requires a listed use-case, and none of its eight areas covers private retail loss prevention; the law-enforcement area (Annex III.6) is confined to systems used by or for law enforcement authorities, which a supermarket checking bags is not. Article 5(1)(d) is likewise not engaged: it bars predicting criminal offences based solely on profiling or personality traits, and expressly does not apply to systems supporting human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity, here, current-cart and checkout anomalies feeding an optional staff check. Article 5(1)(c) fails too: no scoring over a period of time, no unrelated-context or disproportionate detrimental treatment.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Annex III.6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, and explains that a supermarket is not such an authority.
The answer explicitly concludes that a supermarket's tool is not used by or on behalf of law enforcement, and therefore falls outside Annex III.6, regardless of functional similarity.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 continue to apply in full. Because the operator's AI system is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product is, as the base case, subject to third-party conformity assessment, the system is high-risk under Article 6(1)(a) and (b), and Article 43(3) states expressly that the Section 2 requirements apply to such systems and form part of the sectoral assessment. Article 43(3) also governs the opt-out you used: where a Section A Annex I act lets the manufacturer avoid third-party assessment by applying all harmonised standards covering the relevant sectoral requirements, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements of Section 2. Using the opt-out without that AI-side coverage makes the opt-out itself unavailable and the product non-compliant. Article 43(1) and its points (a) to (d) do not assist you: that internal-control route under Annex VI is confined to Annex III point 1 systems. A substantial modification triggers a fresh assessment under Article 43(4).
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing the substance of Article 43(3), second sentence.
The answer explains that the opt-out is available only if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, which is the substance of the third criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents actionable regulatory analysis.
